topics.title: Getting started
topics.html:
Getting started

Choose an available workspace on Home or choose + New analysis to return there. Open a data file and check that its columns, axes and units match the measurement. Inspect the raw curve before applying processing.

Use the document tabs to switch between open analyses. Help → Learning Center opens this manual, technique guidance and the Example Library. Open Example loads the selected dataset in a new document. The library includes synthetic teaching datasets and measured reference examples. Check the provenance and license on each measured example.

Record the settings and ranges you use, and retain a copy of the original measurements.

Your first analysis in about five steps

  1. Open Help → Learning Center → Example Library and select XRD Analysis to see the diffraction peak-width example.
  2. Read the units and expected result, then click Open Example. The example opens in a new analysis tab.
  3. Switch between Plot and Data table. Confirm that the first column is 2θ in degrees and the second column is intensity.
  4. Open Analyze, click Auto-find peaks, and inspect the results. Compare the peak positions against the guide.
  5. Use Export to save a figure or workspace session. Use + New analysis at the far right of the document tab strip to return to Home.
topics.caption: The 3.5 Home screen. Choose a technique card or reopen a saved session.

topics.title: Importing data
topics.html:
Importing data

The spectroscopy reader accepts common numeric text formats including CSV, TSV, TXT, XY, DAT, DPT, ASR and RAW, and Excel XLSX/XLS. Shared import also recognizes ASC in selected workflows. The importer discovers numeric columns, multiple workbook sheets, repeated X/Y pairs and shared-X multiple-Y tables; review the dataset chooser when multiple candidates are found.

  1. Select Home or Data import, or drop supported files onto a compatible workspace.
  2. Check delimiters, decimal notation, headers and numeric values.
  3. Select the intended dataset and inspect axis names and units.
  4. Use Data Table to verify that sample order and numeric values make sense.

Typical data are two columns: independent variable X and measured signal Y. A file extension alone does not guarantee that vendor-specific binary contents can be parsed. LIBS offers folder/ZIP import; 3D/Fluid have additional format-specific constraints.

Troubleshooting

If a plot is blank, verify that a numeric dataset was selected, valid X/Y columns exist and axis limits contain the points. If a file is rejected, export a plain numeric CSV from the instrument's software and retry.

Import your own spectroscopy file

  1. On Home choose the matching technique. Select a file using the file picker, or cancel the picker and drag files into the import page.
  2. A single discovered spectrum normally opens directly. For multiple spectra, click a row to preview the raw trace, then tick the spectra you intend to analyze.
  3. Check column roles and units against the instrument export. Pay particular attention to FT-IR percent transmittance versus absorbance and UV–Vis absorbance versus reflectance.
  4. If a separate reference was measured, select it only after checking compatible units, acquisition settings and overlapping X range.
  5. Click Open [technique] analysis to open the checked data. Keep your original file as a separate record.

topics.title: Workspace and plot controls
topics.html:
Workspace and plot controls

Home, import and analysis documents share a single window. Select the document tab you want to work on. In a spectroscopy document, switch between Plot and Data Table to inspect the figure and values. Use the workspace's analysis controls and history to inspect or revisit operations.

Use the plot toolbar to reset the view, pan and zoom. Use the plot controls to edit axis labels, limits and appearance. Check the selected spectrum before applying processing or adding measurements.

Save a spectroscopy session to reopen the analysis later. Export the figure or data separately for use outside SpectraSuite.

Work on one spectrum at a time

  1. Select the analysis document tab. Select a spectrum in the left Project Data list. Use Prepare above the plot to change the display layout.
  2. Switch between Plot and Data table to compare the figure with the numeric values. If you edit the table, use Apply table to plot to update the plot.
  3. Choose Prepare for processing, Style for axis and legend appearance, Analyze for peaks and measurements, or Annotate for figure labels. Each workflow opens its controls in the right Inspector.
  4. Check Results for derived values and History for recorded operations. Return to the appropriate document tab before continuing another analysis.
topics.caption: The 3.5 spectroscopy document showing its document tabs, plot and Inspector.

topics.title: FT-IR
topics.html:
FT-IR spectroscopy

Phenomenon: infrared absorption excites vibrational transitions whose transition dipole moment changes. Vibrations and group frequencies depend on molecular structure, bonding and environment.

Instrument: IR source → Michelson interferometer → sample → detector → interferogram → Fourier transform → spectrum. Reference/background measurements correct optical and atmospheric contributions but do not eliminate all artifacts.

Imported data: wavenumber (cm⁻¹) versus transmittance (%), absorbance or instrument signal. The conventional wavenumber axis decreases left to right. Absorbance A = −log₁₀(T), where T is fractional transmittance (not percentage); T = %T / 100.

In SpectraSuite: inspect multiple curves using individual/overlay/stack/grid layouts, ALS or manual baseline correction, smoothing, normalization, derivatives, reference subtraction, FT-IR valley selection, selected-range area, Gaussian component fitting and annotations. The peak detector works downward for ordinary transmittance spectra and upward after conversion to absorbance.

Interpretation: a candidate functional-group band is an aid, not proof of chemical identity. Intensities depend on sample thickness, concentration, sampling mode and baseline. Over-smoothing, atmospheric H₂O/CO₂, ATR effects, overlapping bands and improper transmission-to-absorbance conventions are frequent sources of error.

Use the FT-IR example

  1. Open the example and confirm the descending wavenumber axis and the % transmittance scale.
  2. Locate the two downward bands near 2920 and 1720 cm⁻¹. In Analyze, hover over the tools to find the valley selection tool.
  3. Compare the band positions in the raw trace. Confirm the signal representation before comparing band intensities or areas.
topics.caption: Reference plot from the bundled synthetic dataset.

topics.title: XRD
topics.html:
X-ray diffraction

Phenomenon: coherent scattering from periodic crystal planes creates diffraction maxima when Bragg's condition nλ = 2d sin θ is met. Here d is lattice-plane spacing, λ the X-ray wavelength, θ the Bragg angle, and the diffractometer generally records 2θ (degrees).

Instrument: X-ray tube/source → optics → specimen/goniometer → detector → counts or intensity versus 2θ.

In SpectraSuite: upward peak selection, peak labels, local FWHM and a simple Scherrer crystallite-size estimate. The implementation uses D = Kλ/(β cos θ) with K=0.9 and λ=0.15406 nm, converting a FWHM expressed in 2θ degrees to radians; θ is half the 2θ peak position. D is expressed in nm with these wavelength units. Check the source workflow and instrument wavelength before using the numeric result.

Important: coherent-domain (crystallite) size is not necessarily physical particle size. Instrumental width, microstrain, defects, overlapping peaks, shape-factor assumptions and profile shapes can broaden peaks. Automatic instrumental broadening correction, Williamson–Hall, phase identification and Rietveld refinement are not established working features in the inspected source; do not assume they were applied.

Use the XRD example

  1. Locate the peak near 32° in 2θ.
  2. Use Analyze to find the peak and check Show FWHM and grain size. Disable smoothing for comparison with the nominal raw width.
  3. Compare the position and width with the library. Follow the Scherrer guide to see how the width enters a size estimate.
topics.caption: Reference plot from the bundled synthetic dataset.

topics.title: UV-Vis
topics.html:
UV–visible spectroscopy

Phenomenon: photons excite electronic transitions, measured as wavelength-dependent transmission, reflection or absorption. A typical instrument uses UV/visible source(s), a monochromator or dispersive element, sample optics and detector.

Observable: sample and reference intensity determine fractional transmittance T = I/I₀ and absorbance A = −log₁₀ T. Beer–Lambert A = εcl is conditional on a suitable linear absorbing system with defined path length, concentration and negligible scattering.

In SpectraSuite: wavelength to photon energy uses E(eV) = 1239.841984 / λ(nm). Absorbance becomes α(cm⁻¹) = 2.302585093 A / (thickness in μm × 10⁻⁴) only when positive film thickness is supplied; otherwise a relative absorption proxy is used. Kubelka–Munk for reflectance uses F(R)=(1−R)²/(2R), with R fractional reflectance. These proxies are not automatically validated absolute absorption coefficients.

Tauc: the transform is (αE)^r with r = 2 (direct allowed), 1/2 (indirect allowed), 2/3 (direct forbidden) or 1/3 (indirect forbidden) in current code. Fit a researcher-reviewed positive-slope linear interval: Eg = −intercept/slope. The code reports R² and warnings, including R² below 0.98. These are fit diagnostics, not proof of the transition mechanism. Urbach analysis fits ln(absorption) versus energy with EU = 1/slope for positive slope.

Limitations: fit-window selection, scattering, substrate, thickness, reflection assumptions, low-signal edges and transition model affect conclusions. The preprocessing helper can conservatively trim noisy edges, at most a configured fraction, and does not replace raw-data inspection.

Use the UV–Vis example

  1. Check that wavelength is in nm and the signal is absorbance.
  2. Find the band maximum near 530 nm using the plot or data table.
  3. Compare the peak with the expected raw absorbance of about 0.76. Keep the signal in absorbance for this exercise.
topics.caption: Reference plot from the bundled synthetic dataset.

topics.title: Raman
topics.html:
Raman spectroscopy

Phenomenon: most elastically scattered photons are Rayleigh scattered; a small fraction exchanges energy with vibrational modes (Raman scattering). Stokes photons have lower energy than the laser, while anti-Stokes photons have higher energy.

Instrument: monochromatic excitation laser → sample → collection optics → Rayleigh-rejection filters → spectrograph → detector. Displayed Raman shift is typically cm⁻¹, not absolute emitted wavelength.

In SpectraSuite: Raman uses shared processing, peak detection, FWHM, a locally integrated FWHM-interval area, Gaussian fitting and ratios of two distinct detected peak heights. The peak ratio helper uses target shifts and a default matching tolerance of 10 cm⁻¹; a missing or same selected band raises an error. The local area is baseline-relative and is not total band area.

Limitations: fluorescence, laser heating, sample orientation, detector response and overlapping bands complicate interpretation. Do not infer stoichiometry, phase identity or concentration from a raw ratio without calibration and experimental controls.

Use the Raman example

  1. Locate the two bands near 520 and 1000 cm⁻¹.
  2. Notice that the background increases with Raman shift. Compare the original trace with a baseline-corrected trace.
  3. Compare heights only after choosing a consistent background and method.
topics.caption: Reference plot from the bundled synthetic dataset.

topics.title: XPS (preview)
topics.html:
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy — experimental preview

Phenomenon: photoelectric emission from surface atoms. The electron analyzer measures kinetic energy; binding energy is commonly estimated as EB = hν − EK − φ for a consistent analyzer referencing convention.

Instrument: X-ray source → sample in high vacuum → electrostatic electron-energy analyzer → detector → photoelectron spectrum. Survey scans inspect broad elemental signals; high-resolution windows are used to investigate chemical shifts and environments. Charging and referencing are crucial.

In SpectraSuite: generic intensity versus binding-energy plotting, a conventionally decreasing eV axis, generic peak/area tools, processing, overlays, annotations, sessions and export. It is a preview, not a chemically complete XPS interpretation engine.

Not implemented as validated XPS workflows: VAMAS parsing, charge calibration, Shirley/Tougaard background subtraction, constrained chemical-state fits, sensitivity-factor correction and atomic-percent quantification. A generic fitted peak is not a chemical-state assignment.

Use the XPS preview example

  1. Confirm binding energy in eV and intensity in arbitrary units.
  2. Locate the peak near 285 eV and inspect the display axis direction.
  3. Treat the energy as a synthetic peak position. A chemical assignment requires appropriate calibration and supporting evidence.
topics.caption: Reference plot from the bundled synthetic dataset.

topics.title: LIBS (preview)
topics.html:
Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy — experimental preview

Phenomenon: a focused high-intensity laser pulse ablates the target and generates a transient plasma. Excited atoms and ions emit characteristic photons as the plasma cools.

Instrument: pulsed laser → target/plasma → collection optics → spectrometer → gated or ungated detector → emission intensity versus wavelength (usually nm).

In SpectraSuite: import numeric LIBS spectra and select many spectra from folders or ZIP archives, use generic peaks/areas, compare datasets and export. Raw signal is preserved by default. No automated elemental identification or concentration calculation is claimed.

Limits: line overlaps, self-absorption, plasma conditions, matrix effects, atmospheric lines, detector response and wavelength calibration matter. Quantitative LIBS needs validated standards and a calibration strategy. Electron density and plasma temperature workflows are not currently implemented.

Use the LIBS preview example

  1. Check wavelength in nm and intensity in arbitrary units.
  2. Locate the two lines at about 450 and 462 nm. Compare their heights.
  3. Treat these as unassigned synthetic lines. Confirm real assignments with reference lines, spectral resolution and possible interferences.
topics.caption: Reference plot from the bundled synthetic dataset.

topics.title: Baseline and ALS
topics.html:
Baseline correction and ALS

Purpose: estimate slowly varying background so band shape and integrated intensity can be inspected. A poor baseline changes peak heights, widths and areas.

Asymmetric least squares: seek a smooth baseline z by minimizing Σwᵢ(yᵢ−zᵢ)² + λΣ(Δ²zᵢ)², iteratively adjusting weights for observations above and below z. The processing helper defines baseline_als(y, lam=10⁸, p=0.05, itermax=10); the per-spectrum interface stores als_lam as a base-10 logarithm and uses lam=10 ** als_lam (default 8.0), p default 0.05.

In processing order: Savitzky–Golay smoothing if enabled, then baseline subtraction if enabled, then derivatives if selected. The input Y is copied in process_spectrum; inspect session/workspace state before claiming unconditional recovery across every workflow.

Use with care: peak crowding, asymmetric envelopes and strong background changes can make the baseline physically implausible. Preserve raw measurements and export settings alongside processed results.

Compare a corrected curve with its raw data

  1. Open the Raman example and note the upward slope between the peaks.
  2. On the raw view, identify background-only regions away from peaks. Apply a baseline method using the workspace controls and compare corrected and raw curves.
  3. Check that the baseline follows the background without cutting into broad features. Record the method and settings used, especially before comparing areas or ratios.

topics.title: Smoothing and derivatives
topics.html:
Savitzky–Golay smoothing and derivatives

A local polynomial is fitted within a moving window to reduce high-frequency noise while retaining polynomial-like curve structure. Smoothing can still suppress narrow peaks or shift extrema if the window is too large.

In SpectraSuite's process_spectrum helper: smooth defaults to 0 (off). When positive, the requested window is forced odd and at least five samples; polynomial order is 3; the transform is applied only when data length exceeds the window. First and second derivatives use Savitzky–Golay order 3, the selected smoothing window or 5 if smoothing is off, with derivative order 1 or 2. The function does not specify a wavelength/sample-spacing delta, so these derivatives are with respect to sample index unless another workflow rescales them.

Scientific caution: sample spacing, noisy boundaries and nonuniform X matter. Compare processed and raw curves, and avoid treating a smoothed signal as a better experimental measurement merely because it looks cleaner.

Check whether smoothing changes a measurement

  1. Use the unsmoothed trace as a reference. Record the position and width of a representative peak.
  2. Increase the smoothing window in small increments. Recheck that peak and a nearby shoulder at the same zoom.
  3. Keep the smallest window that makes the measurement more stable. Record the window in samples and consider the spacing between X values.

topics.title: Reference subtraction and trimming
topics.html:
Reference subtraction and noisy-edge trimming

Reference subtraction removes a separately measured component only when acquisition modes, units and signal scales are compatible. In spectral_preprocessing.subtract_reference the reference is sorted in X, interpolated onto the sample X positions and subtracted with a configurable multiplier (default 1). NumPy interpolation uses boundary values outside the reference range; overlapping domains should be checked before interpreting the result.

The optical trim_noisy_edges helper compares local end-region point-to-point variation against a central robust noise scale; its default maximum_fraction is 0.10 and curves under 50 finite points are returned untrimmed. It may discard suspect edge samples, so retain original measurement files and verify that meaningful spectral structure was not removed.

topics.title: Peak detection, area and FWHM
topics.html:
Peak detection, area and FWHM

A local maximum/minimum is a feature of the supplied processed signal, not a chemical assignment. The shared detector smooths a copy for detection, estimates robust span and derivative noise, and uses prominence at least max(0.08 × robust span, 6 × noise, machine epsilon) when prominence is automatic. Conventional FT-IR transmittance valleys are detected downward; other workflows predominantly detect upward features.

FWHM: the distance between the two half-height crossings, after defining the peak and baseline. Widths must be converted to physical X units rather than conflated with sample indices. Peak area is an integral over a specified interval, often via numerical trapezoids; units are signal × X unit and results depend on baseline, clipping and interval.

Raman specific: peak_widths uses relative height 0.5, with interpolation of crossings onto X. The local area is trapezoidal integration of the positive signal above a straight baseline connecting those crossings. It is not full-band area.

Review automatic peak picks

  1. Start with Analyze → Auto-find peaks and note the detected positions.
  2. Compare markers with the original trace. Check weak peaks, shoulders and edge artifacts individually.
  3. Use the local background when interpreting peak height or width. Record the baseline and integration interval alongside any reported area.

topics.title: Scherrer crystallite size
topics.html:
Scherrer crystallite-size calculation

Equation: D = Kλ/(β cos θ). D is the coherent diffraction-domain size; K is dimensionless shape factor; λ and D share the same length unit; β is broadening in radians of 2θ; and θ is half the peak position angle. For λ = 0.15406 nm and K = 0.9, D is in nm.

In the source snapshot the XRD workflow is a simple FWHM-based Scherrer estimate. It does not automatically remove instrumental broadening or strain broadening, and the result should not be called measured particle diameter. Compare instrument standards, line-shape corrections and several reflections independently before making structural claims.

Reference: Patterson, A. L. (1939), The Scherrer Formula for X-Ray Particle Size Determination, Physical Review 56, 978–982.

Worked estimate using the synthetic XRD peak

  1. The example's first peak is at 2θ ≈ 32°, so the Bragg angle θ is about 16°. Its nominal raw FWHM is 1.18° in 2θ.
  2. Convert the width to radians, β ≈ 1.18 × π / 180 ≈ 0.0206 rad. The width stays a width in 2θ. Halve the peak position to obtain θ.
  3. For illustration, use K = 0.9 and λ = 0.15406 nm. D = Kλ / (β cos θ) gives about 7.0 nm before any instrumental correction.
  4. The example uses a Gaussian teaching curve. In a measured sample, verify the wavelength, shape factor, instrumental contribution and peak overlap before interpreting a size.
topics.caption: The two marked crossings define the full width at half maximum of the synthetic XRD peak.

topics.title: Tauc analysis
topics.html:
Tauc and Urbach analysis

The Tauc model linearizes an assumed absorption-edge relation. SpectraSuite constructs (αE)^r with transition-specific exponent r and fits ordinate = mE + b. The extrapolated energy intercept is Eg = −b/m. Current code rejects non-positive slopes and non-physical intercepts, reports R² and a propagated regression uncertainty where obtainable, and warns on poorly linear or excessive-extrapolation intervals.

Urbach energy follows α(E) ∝ exp(E/EU) over an appropriate exponential tail; fit ln α versus E and compute EU = 1/m for positive slope. The relative-absorption proxy, diffuse-reflectance transform and selected energy interval may invalidate naive comparisons between samples.

References: Tauc, J., Grigorovici, R., and Vancu, A. (1966), Physica Status Solidi 15, 627–637; Urbach, F. (1953), Physical Review 92, 1324.

From a measured spectrum to a defensible fit

  1. Open Analyze → UV-Vis band-gap and Urbach analysis on data with an appropriate absorption edge.
  2. Set the actual input axis and signal types. Choose a transition model supported by the material or literature.
  3. Use Suggest Tauc range as a starting point. Examine the transformed curve and test nearby fit windows, then use Calculate / refresh.
  4. Report the chosen model, fit range, energy intercept and sensitivity to the interval. The bundled UV–Vis absorption-band example is for locating a maximum, not for determining a band gap.

topics.title: Deconvolution and fitting
topics.html:
Peak fitting and deconvolution

Fitting approximates the observed signal as baseline plus parameterized peaks. A Gaussian curve is y(x)=A exp[−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)] with FWHM = 2√(2 ln 2)σ. Lorentzian and Voigt families reflect different tail and broadening assumptions; their scientific introduction does not establish that a corresponding SpectraSuite fitter exists.

Implemented scope: Gaussian component fitting/deconvolution is documented in shared FT-IR, UV-Vis and Raman workflows. Do not claim Lorentzian, Voigt or pseudo-Voigt fitting as working until source and tests confirm it.

Interpretation: components can be mathematically nonunique. Choose plausible model complexity, fit region and background, inspect residuals, and do not equate a fitted component with an independently confirmed species.

topics.title: From instrument to interpretation
topics.html:
From measurement to interpretation

Physical phenomenon → instrument measurement → imported X/Y data → processing → quantitative analysis → scientific interpretation.

The instrument converts a physical response into detector signals and instrument software may already transform or normalize them. Confirm whether a file is raw counts, transmittance, absorbance, diffraction intensity, photoelectron counts or plasma emission. SpectraSuite reads and analyzes supplied datasets; it does not control the instrument or reconstruct missing calibration/metadata.

Processing is not a new experimental measurement. Fit accuracy is not necessarily physical validity. Record the original data, preparation, instrument settings, sample geometry, processing parameters, fit interval, units and uncertainty sources when drawing conclusions.

topics.title: Equations used by SpectraSuite
topics.html:
Equations and scientific references

Bragg: nλ=2d sinθ (λ,d lengths; θ half of diffraction 2θ).

Scherrer: D=Kλ/(β cosθ); broadening β in radians, K dimensionless.

Absorbance: A=−log₁₀ T, T fractional transmittance.

Kubelka–Munk: F(R)=(1−R)²/(2R), R fractional diffuse reflectance, subject to scattering and optical-model assumptions.

Tauc: fit (αE)^r = mE+b, Eg=−b/m under assumed transition and valid edge region.

Urbach: lnα = E/EU + constant in selected tail region.

Gaussian: A exp[−(x−μ)²/(2σ²)].

Further reading

  1. Griffiths & de Haseth, Fourier Transform Infrared Spectrometry, 2nd ed., Wiley (2007).
  2. Cullity & Stock, Elements of X-Ray Diffraction, 3rd ed., Prentice Hall (2001).
  3. Patterson (1939), Physical Review 56, 978–982, doi:10.1103/PhysRev.56.978.
  4. Hollas, Modern Spectroscopy, 4th ed., Wiley (2004).
  5. Tauc, Grigorovici & Vancu (1966), physica status solidi (b) 15, 627–637, doi:10.1002/pssb.19660150224.
  6. Urbach (1953), Physical Review 92, 1324.
  7. Savitzky & Golay (1964), Analytical Chemistry 36, 1627–1639, doi:10.1021/ac60214a047.
  8. Eilers & Boelens (2005), Baseline Correction with Asymmetric Least Squares, Leiden University report.
  9. Brundle, Evans & Wilson (eds.), Encyclopedia of Materials Characterization, Butterworth-Heinemann (1992).
  10. Cremers & Radziemski, Handbook of Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy, 2nd ed., Wiley (2013).

These works explain underlying science; implementations and defaults must be checked against SpectraSuite code rather than inferred from textbooks.

topics.title: Image to Data digitizer
topics.html:
Image to Data digitizer

The digitizer extracts approximate XY values from an existing graph image, not instrument-native raw data. Open Image to Data and import a PNG, JPEG, BMP, TIFF or WebP through file selection, clipboard or drag/drop.

  1. Enter X0, X1, Y0 and Y1 calibration values and appropriate axis units; use logarithmic calibration only where valid and all relevant values are positive.
  2. Click the axis corner (X0,Y0), the second X-axis point (X1,Y0), then the third Y-axis point (X0,Y1). Green plus signs mark calibration points.
  3. Click red data points manually, or select automatic curve-color tracing and click the intended curve to trace its connected color component.
  4. Review and correct erroneous points, use Undo or recalibrate as needed.
  5. Send extracted data to the compatible workspace or export CSV plus its calibration JSON provenance file.

Rotated or reversed axes can be calibrated. Lines touching text, grids, axes, or multiple objects of similar color can be traced incorrectly. Image resolution, perspective distortion and manual calibration bound accuracy; do not claim the digitizer recovers instrument precision.

Check calibration before exporting

  1. Choose axes values from readable ticks, using reference points far enough apart to reduce the effect of click error.
  2. Trace a few points first. Compare a recovered coordinate against a visible tick or known point, then finish tracing.
  3. Keep the image and the CSV with its calibration metadata. Record that the data were digitized from an image.

topics.title: Exporting data and figures
topics.html:
Exporting figures, data and reports

Select the active plot/workspace, then open Export. Available output depends on the workspace. Shared figure output supports PDF/SVG vector formats and PNG/JPG/TIFF raster formats. PDF/SVG preserve scalable graphics; DPI principally affects raster output or embedded raster elements.

  1. Choose output format and figure dimensions.
  2. Set the resolution when exporting a raster image; supported presets include 150, 300, 600 and 1200 DPI.
  3. Choose whether the background should be transparent when the chosen format permits it (JPG does not).
  4. Review the preview and any warnings.
  5. Save and verify the resulting file before submitting figures for publication.

The Trim empty outer margins option can reduce final dimensions below the requested width and height. Turn it off for exact layout dimensions. Supported batch/report export may include individual plots, processed CSV, JSON metadata, results and a PDF report, with dataset selection as appropriate. Figure export does not automatically establish that processing or scientific interpretation is correct.

Choose the right deliverable

  1. Use Save figure… for a standalone graph. Use PDF or SVG when the destination accepts vectors, or PNG/TIFF when a raster figure is required.
  2. Use Export data / results bundle… when collaborators need numeric values or analysis results. Check the exported columns and units in an independent viewer.
  3. Use Save workspace session… when you need to continue editing later.

topics.title: Sessions and history
topics.html:
Sessions, history and provenance

Spectroscopy sessions use structured JSON to preserve supported document state and analysis information. Use the workspace's Save Session command and keep the original experimental files independently. When opening a saved session, verify imported spectrum values, axis direction, processing selections, annotations and results before reusing them.

History supports understanding and in some contexts undoing analysis actions. It is not a tamper-proof laboratory audit trail. A session is not an instrument-native raw-data archive, nor a guarantee of identical behavior across arbitrary future versions. For reproducibility, retain sample identifiers, instrument method, calibration, measurement date, raw files and the export manifest separately.

Save, reopen and verify a session

  1. In the active spectroscopy document, choose Export → Save workspace session… and save the JSON.
  2. From Home choose Open saved session… and select the JSON. Verify the technique, series names, labels, annotations and results you intend to use.
  3. Export the figure or results bundle separately and keep it with the original data and session JSON.

topics.title: Troubleshooting
topics.html:
Troubleshooting checklist

Empty plot: confirm that selected data contain finite numeric X/Y values; inspect column roles and axis limits. Wrong axis: verify imported units and conventional technique direction before manually reversing axes. Import rejected: re-export a plain numeric delimited file; some vendor-specific binary files are not supported.

Overly flat or distorted peaks: disable smoothing, normalization or baseline correction to compare against original data. Unexpected area: examine interval limits, whether the operation integrates a local FWHM region, baseline and units. Invalid Tauc fit: revisit absorption-signal type, material transition model, fit interval and slope. Scherrer estimate looks implausible: check wavelength, FWHM, degrees-to-radians conversion, instrumental broadening and peak overlap.

Export does not match dimensions: disable outer-margin trimming. Digitized curve incorrect: recalibrate axes and choose a clean image or manual points. Source launch fails: confirm a supported Python interpreter and required dependencies; a packaged installer has different requirements. Update checks need internet, but scientific analysis does not.

topics.title: Normalization and transforms
topics.html:
Normalization, signal transforms and subtraction

Normalization rescales a curve to facilitate shape comparison, but changes absolute peak heights and can invalidate comparisons of intensity, concentration or area when a common calibrated response is required. Confirm the selected normalization procedure in the active processing dialog; the inspected low-level helper shown here does not define a global normalization constant or default for all techniques.

FT-IR transmittance and absorbance are different signal representations; peak direction is reversed by conversion, and logarithms require positive transmission. UV-Vis transformations require precise signal identity (fraction versus percent). Reflectance-to-Kubelka–Munk should not be treated as a measured absorption coefficient without appropriate scattering assumptions. Reference subtraction should be used only with compatible X units and measurement conditions.

topics.title: Urbach energy
topics.html:
Urbach energy from absorption tails

In materials showing an exponential absorption tail, α(E)=α₀ exp(E/EU) over a suitable limited energy region. Taking logarithms gives lnα = constant + E/EU, so fitting positive absorption in the selected interval yields EU=1/m where m is the fitted positive slope in eV⁻¹. SpectraSuite computes this from sorted, finite data via a linear regression of ln(absorption) against energy.

Use a physically plausible region in the exponential tail; an arbitrary fitted slope is not necessarily an Urbach energy. Instrument floor, scattering, nonzero baseline, optical thickness, and changes in phase or defect structure may influence the value.

Reference: Urbach, F., The Long-Wavelength Edge of Photographic Sensitivity and of the Electronic Absorption of Solids, Physical Review 92 (1953) 1324.

topics.title: Kubelka–Munk transform
topics.html:
Kubelka–Munk diffuse reflectance model

For an optically thick, diffuse-scattering sample under an appropriate two-flux model, F(R∞)=(1−R∞)²/(2R∞) can relate absorption and scattering coefficients. R must be fractional reflectance, not percent. The implemented transform accepts fraction or percentage input through explicit signal typing.

The proportionality to absorption assumes scattering properties suitable for the model, adequate sample thickness and proper referencing. Mirror-like reflection, transparency, wavelength-varying scattering and sample packing can invalidate simplistic optical-band-gap treatment. Do not interpret F(R) as an independently measured α(cm⁻¹).

topics.title: FWHM interpretation
topics.html:
Full width at half maximum (FWHM)

FWHM is the distance on the independent-variable axis between two crossings at half the feature height relative to the designated local baseline. An isolated Gaussian with standard deviation σ has FWHM = 2√(2ln2) σ; other line shapes have different parameter-width relationships.

It measures apparent spectral breadth, not one universal material property. Baseline placement, overlap, instrument resolution, smoothing, sampling step and units all matter. For XRD, a size estimate based on FWHM requires degrees-to-radians conversion and should account for instrumental/strain contributions for physically reliable inference. For Raman, SpectraSuite interpolates crossing positions onto Raman-shift values rather than reporting sample-index widths.

Read the half-height construction

  1. Identify a local background and peak maximum. The half-height level is background + half of the peak height above that background.
  2. Find where the profile crosses this level on both sides of the peak. The difference between the two X coordinates is the FWHM.
  3. Check whether smoothing, overlapping peaks or unequal backgrounds make either crossing unreliable.

General 2D plotting

A 2D plot maps an independent variable to one or more responses. Use one curve per response with compatible units.

Plot the calibration example

  1. Check the X mapping for concentration and the Y mapping for absorbance.
  2. Use Plot / refresh after changing mappings. Check the axis units and the intercept.
  3. Compare the points with the straight-line response. Treat the bundled points as illustrative rather than an experimental calibration.

topics.title: General 3D plotting
topics.html:
General 3D plotting

A 3D plot maps an X and Y location to a Z value. A scatter view shows measured points. A surface or contour connects or interpolates samples and can imply structure between them.

Plot the height-field example

  1. Check the X, Y and Z mappings and confirm all three axes are in millimetres.
  2. Compare a point view with a surface view using the plot-type selector.
  3. Rotate the view to see the central mound. Compare the height at the origin with the 5 mm expected value.

topics.title: Fluid Dynamics Plotter (Preview)
topics.html:
Fluid Dynamics Plotter (Preview)

A flow-field table stores X and Y coordinates with quantities such as velocity, pressure or temperature. Check the grid, units and variable names before interpreting a contour or profile.

Plot the velocity-profile example

  1. Select Speed (m/s) as the plotted variable and inspect the color scale.
  2. Choose Profile along Y, set the slice near the middle of X, then select Plot selected.
  3. The profile peaks near the center of Y and reaches zero at both outer boundaries. Check the distance units before reporting a gradient.
